title: Berlin Street Signs - FAQ
subtitle: The rules, the numbers, the plaques and the renamings.

items.q: Why do Berlin street signs look the way they do?
items.a: Berlin's regulation on street naming, the **AV Benennung**, fixes the design: **black letters on a light, reflective panel**, Berlin's **own typeface** rather than DIN 1451, and a **cast aluminium frame** with a field for a house-number plate.

items.q: What does the small plate with numbers mean?
items.a: It shows the **house numbers on that stretch of the street**, so you can see before you walk whether your number is on this block. Berlin calls them **Grundstücksnummern**, because empty plots are numbered too.

items.q: How are house numbers ordered in Berlin?
items.a: Two systems are still in use. Older streets often use **horseshoe numbering**: up one side and back down the other, so the highest number faces number 1. Since the **1975** ordinance, new numbering is **odd on the left, even on the right**, rising away from the old centre.

items.q: What is the plaque under some street signs?
items.a: An **Erläuterungsschild**, an explanatory plaque. It is optional and usually tells you in up to **three lines** who the street is named after, sometimes with three more about their work.

items.q: Why is there a crossed-out sign under the new name?
items.a: After a renaming, Berlin leaves the old sign up for **six months**, struck through in red but readable, so everyone can get used to the new name.

items.q: Can I buy a real Berlin street sign?
items.a: Not off a pole: a street sign belongs to the city, and taking one is **theft**. I found no official sale of old Berlin signs. What you can buy is a sign **in the style** of a Berlin street sign with your own name, made for an indoor wall.

items.q: How many streets does Berlin have?
items.a: About **11,480**, counting squares, bridges and private streets, according to the **Amt für Statistik Berlin-Brandenburg**. The most common name is **Waldstraße**, eleven times.
